Infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and reviewable.
Terraform: providers, resources and data sources, with remote, locked state.
GitOps (Argo CD, Flux) syncs Kubernetes from Git.

check.q: Why must Terraform state be remote and locked?
check.a: So a team shares one source of truth and two applies cannot run at once.

check.q: What does 'disposability' mean for a service?
check.a: It starts fast and shuts down gracefully, so instances can be killed and replaced at any time.

check.q: What is GitOps?
check.a: The cluster's desired state lives in Git and an agent applies it continuously.

takeaways: Some companies run AI-assisted coding rounds; they grade how you decompose, prompt, verify and test, not typing speed.
Expect a small multi-file codebase and features or bugs to handle with an AI tool.
AI-off rounds still exist; fundamentals and explaining your reasoning still matter.
Ask the recruiter which tools are allowed and practise reading unfamiliar code fast.

check.q: What do AI-assisted rounds grade?
check.a: Problem decomposition, precise prompting, verification of every line, testing, and judgement.

check.q: What should you ask the recruiter beforehand?
check.a: Whether AI tools are allowed and which ones, and the format of the round.

check.q: What habit matters most with AI help?
check.a: Verifying output with tests and reading every line before accepting it.

takeaways: Clarify the problem yourself before opening the AI.
Decompose, then prompt with constraints (language, signatures, edge cases, style).
Read and verify every line; choose the test cases yourself.
Narrate as you go, and when something fails, form a hypothesis before asking the AI.

check.q: Why state the approach yourself before prompting?
check.a: It shows the thinking is yours and keeps the AI's output on your design.

check.q: Who should choose the test cases?
check.a: You, so the AI cannot hide its own mistakes in its own tests.

check.q: What goes into a good prompt in an interview?
check.a: The exact task, constraints, signatures, edge cases and what not to change.

takeaways: Check every time for hallucinated or outdated APIs and packages (slopsquatting).
Look for boundary errors, missing edge cases, concurrency bugs, security holes and weak error handling.
Money and time are classic traps: floating point and time zones.
Read the diff, not the explanation; ask 'what happens when...?'; run your own test.

check.q: What is slopsquatting?
check.a: Attackers register package names that AI tools hallucinate, so installing them pulls malware.

check.q: Give an example of an outdated API an AI might suggest.
check.a: `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` or `javax.persistence` in a Spring Boot 3+ project.

check.q: Name a concurrency bug AI often writes.
check.a: Get-then-put on a shared map, which loses updates.

takeaways: Tools come as inline completion, chat, agents and review bots; each needs a different level of oversight.
AI helps most with reading code, boilerplate, tests, migrations and first drafts.
Be careful with security-sensitive code, concurrency, transactions and performance-critical paths.
Follow data policies (no secrets or customer data in prompts) and keep your own skills sharp.

check.q: Where should you be most careful using AI code?
check.a: Security, concurrency and transactions, and performance-critical paths.

check.q: What must never go into a prompt?
check.a: Secrets and customer data, unless the tool is approved for it.

check.q: How do you keep your skills sharp?
check.a: Write critical parts yourself, understand everything you merge, and practise without the tool.

takeaways: Signs of unattended generated code: unused abstractions, invented APIs, inconsistent style, tests that assert nothing.
Review in order: intent, tests, interfaces and data, correctness hotspots, security, operability, simplicity, style.
Pull the branch and run it; check every new import and dependency.
Ask the author to explain it; rank findings by production risk.

check.q: What is a red flag in AI-written tests?
check.a: Tests that only check mocks were called, or would pass whatever the code does.

check.q: Why check every new dependency?
check.a: It may be hallucinated, typo-squatted, unmaintained or vulnerable.

check.q: What is a fair team norm for AI-generated PRs?
check.a: The author must be able to explain every line, and the PR is held to the same review bar.

takeaways: Tokens, context window, input vs output tokens, temperature and system prompts are the core vocabulary.
LLMs hallucinate; ground answers with RAG (embed, retrieve, add to the prompt) and cite sources.
Cost and latency scale with tokens, especially output tokens; do the arithmetic.
Tool calling: the model asks your code to run a function, and your code decides and executes.

check.q: What is RAG?
check.a: Retrieve relevant documents (usually by embedding similarity) and add them to the prompt so the model answers from them.

check.q: Why do output tokens matter more for latency?
check.a: They are generated one at a time, so long answers take longer and usually cost more per token.

check.q: Who executes a tool call?
check.a: Your application; the model only requests it.

takeaways: Treat the LLM like any unreliable remote dependency: timeouts, limited retries, circuit breaker and a fallback.
Control cost with quotas, caching and model choice; move slow work to async jobs.
Defend against direct and indirect prompt injection; give tools least privilege and require human confirmation for risky actions.
Treat output as untrusted, keep secrets and unneeded personal data out of prompts, and monitor quality.

check.q: What is indirect prompt injection?
check.a: Malicious instructions hidden in content the model reads, such as a retrieved document or email.

check.q: Why treat LLM output as untrusted?
check.a: It can be wrong or manipulated; validate it before acting or rendering it.

check.q: Name three resilience controls for an LLM call.
check.a: Timeout, circuit breaker and a fallback response.

takeaways: Start with the use case and success metric, and ask whether an LLM is needed at all.
Cover data and retrieval, model and prompting, serving, safety and privacy, evaluation, cost and latency, operations.
Enforce permissions at retrieval time so users see only documents they may access.
Handle freshness and grounding, and say how you evaluate quality.

check.q: Where must permissions be enforced in a RAG system?
check.a: At retrieval, so documents a user may not see never reach the prompt.

check.q: What is the first question in AI system design?
check.a: What problem and metric, and is an LLM needed at all?

check.q: How do you evaluate a RAG assistant?
check.a: A test set of questions with expected answers, measuring retrieval quality and answer faithfulness, plus user feedback.

takeaways: Senior means larger scope, handling ambiguity, technical judgement, ownership after release, and making others better.
Interviews probe it through system design, project deep dives, behavioral follow-ups, code review and debugging.
Translate service-company work into product language: decisions you made, trade-offs, and measured outcomes.
Start the behaviours now; they become your interview stories.

check.q: Name three dimensions that change from mid-level to senior.
check.a: Scope, handling ambiguity, influence and multiplying others; also ownership and judgement.

check.q: How do you describe client work in product terms?
check.a: Focus on what you decided and why, the trade-offs, and the measurable result.

check.q: What does 'ownership after release' mean?
check.a: Watching metrics, fixing issues and improving the feature after it ships, not stopping at merge.

takeaways: Write a design doc when a change is risky, cross-team, or hard to reverse.
Template: context, problem, goals and non-goals, proposal, alternatives, cross-cutting concerns, rollout, risks.
Alternatives with honest trade-offs are the most valuable part.
Keep it short with a summary first, and ask specific reviewers specific questions.

check.q: Why list non-goals?
check.a: They set scope and stop the discussion drifting.

check.q: What is the most valuable section of a design doc?
check.a: Alternatives and the reasons for choosing one.

check.q: When is a design doc unnecessary?
check.a: For small, easily reversible changes inside one team.

takeaways: Clarify the outcome, slice vertically, find unknowns and spike them.
Estimate in ranges and add the invisible work: tests, reviews, rollout, monitoring.
Sequence by risk so surprises appear early.
Communicate confidence and re-estimate as you learn; with a fixed date, negotiate scope.

check.q: Why slice work vertically?
check.a: Each slice delivers something usable end to end and exposes integration risk early.

check.q: What is a spike?
check.a: A short, time-boxed investigation to reduce an unknown before estimating.

check.q: The date is fixed and the work does not fit. What do you do?
check.a: Cut or phase scope, explicitly agreed with stakeholders.

takeaways: Frame a trade-off: the decision and constraint, 2-4 real options, criteria that matter, an honest comparison.
Weigh reversibility: decide fast on reversible choices and carefully on irreversible ones; record the decision in an ADR.
Disagree with evidence, make the idea cheap to test, and separate the person from the idea.
Escalate transparently if needed, then disagree and commit.

check.q: What is an ADR?
check.a: An architecture decision record: a short note of a decision, its context and consequences.

check.q: How do you push back on a senior engineer?
check.a: Understand their reasons, bring data, propose a cheap experiment, and commit once decided.

check.q: Why does reversibility matter?
check.a: Reversible decisions can be made quickly; irreversible ones deserve more analysis.

takeaways: Code review is for correctness and safety, design, knowledge sharing and consistency.
Review in risk order, label comments (blocker vs nit), explain why, and praise specifically.
Keep PRs small, review quickly, and move big discussions to a call.
Mentor with onboarding plans and pairing; raise the bar with automation, not policing.

check.q: Why label review comments?
check.a: So the author knows what must change (blocker) and what is optional (nit).

check.q: How do you raise code quality without policing?
check.a: Automate the checks (linters, CI), share examples, and lead by example.

check.q: Name a practical mentoring technique.
check.a: Pair programming, or a structured onboarding plan with a first small task.

takeaways: Declare incidents early and assign roles: incident commander, experts, communications, scribe.
Mitigate first, investigate second.
Update stakeholders on a regular cadence with impact, status and next update time.
Run blameless postmortems with owned action items; tell incident stories with your actions and the prevention.

check.q: Why declare an incident early?
check.a: It brings the right people and process in quickly; downgrading later is cheap.

check.q: What goes in an incident status update?
check.a: Impact, current status, what is being done, and when the next update will come.

check.q: How should an incident story end in an interview?
check.a: With what changed afterwards so it cannot happen the same way again.

takeaways: Know your audience and put the bottom line up front.
Send regular status updates and raise risks early: no surprises.
Say no well: acknowledge the goal, explain the cost, offer alternatives, and let them decide.
Write for leadership in outcomes and decisions, not technical detail.

check.q: What is BLUF?
check.a: Bottom line up front: state the conclusion or request first.

check.q: How do you say no to a stakeholder?
check.a: Acknowledge the goal, explain the cost, offer alternatives, and let them choose.

check.q: When should you raise a risk?
check.a: As soon as it is likely enough to matter, not when it has already happened.

takeaways: Structure 10-12 minutes: context, constraints, options, decision, a failure you handled, results and lessons.
Be clear about your own role versus the team's.
Behavioral answers: stakes (20%), actions (60%), outcome (20%).
Build a story bank and rehearse the probes: why not X, what would you change, how did you measure it.

check.q: What does the stakes-action-outcome split look like?
check.a: About 20% stakes, 60% your actions, 20% measured outcome.

check.q: What probe should you always prepare for?
check.a: Why you chose this design over the alternatives, and what you would change now.

check.q: What is the most common deep-dive mistake?
check.a: Describing what the team did without making your own decisions and contribution clear.

takeaways: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism: give a one-line example of each from real code.
Overriding: same signature, covariant return, no weaker access, no broader checked exceptions; resolved at runtime.
Prefer composition over inheritance; use an interface for a capability and an abstract class for shared state.

check.q: Can an overriding method throw a broader checked exception?
check.a: No; it may throw the same, narrower or none.

check.q: Compile-time vs runtime polymorphism?
check.a: Overloading is chosen by the compiler from argument types; overriding is chosen at runtime from the object's type.

check.q: When an abstract class over an interface?
check.a: When implementations share state or constructor logic.

takeaways: Equal objects must have equal hash codes; override equals and hashCode together.
Never mutate a field used in hashCode while the object is a key in a HashMap or HashSet.
For JPA entities, base equality on a stable business key or the id with care, not on all fields.

check.q: Override only equals: what breaks?
check.a: Hash collections put equal objects in different buckets, so lookups and dedupe fail.

check.q: Why are mutable keys dangerous?
check.a: Changing the key changes its hash, so the entry can no longer be found.

check.q: Shallow vs deep copy?
check.a: Shallow copies references to the same nested objects; deep copies the nested objects too.

takeaways: HashMap: array of buckets, index from the spread hash, chains become red-black trees past 8, resize doubles at 75% full.
LinkedHashMap keeps insertion or access order (the basis of an LRU cache); TreeMap keeps keys sorted in O(log n).
ArrayList for almost everything; fail-fast iterators throw ConcurrentModificationException on outside changes.

check.q: When does a default HashMap first resize?
check.a: When the 13th entry is added: capacity 16 × load factor 0.75 = 12.

check.q: Why treeify a bucket?
check.a: So a heavily colliding bucket costs O(log n) instead of O(n).

check.q: How do you build an LRU cache from the JDK?
check.a: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true and removeEldestEntry.

takeaways: ConcurrentHashMap: lock-free reads, CAS into empty bins, a lock on the bin head otherwise; no global lock.
Use its atomic compound methods (`compute`, `merge`, `putIfAbsent`) instead of get-then-put.
Pick the concurrent collection by access pattern: CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly lists, BlockingQueue for producer-consumer.

check.q: Why no null keys or values?
check.a: A null from get could not tell 'absent' from 'mapped to null' without racing.

check.q: Java 7 vs Java 8 ConcurrentHashMap?
check.a: Java 7 locked 16 segments; Java 8 uses CAS and per-bin locks.

check.q: Which queue for producer-consumer?
check.a: A bounded BlockingQueue such as ArrayBlockingQueue, using put and take.

takeaways: A lambda implements a functional interface; captured local variables must be effectively final.
Know Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier and method references.
Optional is a return type for 'may be absent': not for fields or parameters; prefer orElseGet for expensive defaults.

check.q: Why must captured variables be effectively final?
check.a: The lambda copies the value; allowing changes would make the copy and the variable disagree.

check.q: orElse vs orElseGet?
check.a: orElse always evaluates its argument; orElseGet calls the supplier only when empty.

check.q: Name the four core functional interfaces.
check.a: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier.

takeaways: A stream is source, lazy intermediate operations, then one terminal operation.
groupingBy with a downstream collector (counting, averaging, mapping, maxBy) solves most coding questions.
Parallel streams help only for large, CPU-bound, independent work; never with shared mutable state.

check.q: When does a stream pipeline actually run?
check.a: Only when a terminal operation is called.

check.q: Count words by frequency with streams?
check.a: `groupingBy(Function.identity(), counting())`.

check.q: Why can parallel streams be slower?
check.a: Splitting and merging overhead, shared common pool, and contention on shared state.

takeaways: Records for data carriers, sealed types for closed hierarchies, pattern matching for switch to handle each case.
Virtual threads (21) make blocking I/O code scale; they do not speed up CPU work.
Java 25 is the newest LTS: scoped values, compact source files, flexible constructor bodies.

check.q: What does a record generate?
check.a: A canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString for its components.

check.q: Why do sealed types pair well with switch?
check.a: The compiler knows every subtype, so a switch can be exhaustive without default.

check.q: When do virtual threads not help?
check.a: CPU-bound work, or when a pool or rate limit downstream caps throughput anyway.

takeaways: synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility; volatile gives visibility and ordering only, not atomicity.
happens-before is the rule: unlock before lock, volatile write before read, start before the thread's actions.
wait releases the monitor, sleep does not; interrupt to stop a blocked thread cooperatively.

check.q: Is `count++` on a volatile int thread-safe?
check.a: No; it is read-modify-write. Use AtomicInteger or a lock.

check.q: sleep vs wait?
check.a: sleep pauses without releasing locks; wait releases the monitor and waits for notify.

check.q: Why double-checked locking needs volatile?
check.a: Without it another thread may see a partly constructed instance.

takeaways: Use bounded ThreadPoolExecutors with a rejection policy; know core size, max size, queue and keep-alive.
CompletableFuture composes async work; pass your own executor instead of the common pool for I/O.
Deadlock needs four conditions; break one, usually by acquiring locks in a fixed order or with tryLock timeouts.

check.q: When does a ThreadPoolExecutor create threads beyond core size?
check.a: Only when the queue is full; with an unbounded queue it never does.

check.q: Name the four deadlock conditions.
check.a: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.

check.q: thenApply vs thenCompose?
check.a: thenApply maps the result; thenCompose chains another CompletableFuture without nesting.

takeaways: Memory areas: heap (objects), stack per thread, metaspace (class metadata), plus native memory.
Class loaders delegate to the parent first (bootstrap, platform, application).
GC reclaims objects unreachable from GC roots; most objects die young, so collectors are generational.

check.q: StackOverflowError vs OutOfMemoryError?
check.a: Stack overflow is too-deep recursion on one thread's stack; OOM is the heap (or metaspace) running out.

check.q: What is a GC root?
check.a: A reference the GC starts from: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references.

check.q: Name a common cause of Java memory leaks.
check.a: Objects kept reachable, e.g. a static map or cache that only grows, or unremoved listeners.

takeaways: The container creates and wires beans; constructor injection is the default choice.
ApplicationContext adds events, i18n and eager singleton creation on top of BeanFactory.
Resolve ambiguity with @Primary or @Qualifier; redesign circular dependencies instead of allowing them.

check.q: Why constructor injection?
check.a: Final, explicit, testable dependencies and early failure on cycles.

check.q: @Primary vs @Qualifier?
check.a: @Primary sets a default; @Qualifier picks a bean at the injection point and wins.

check.q: How do you fix a circular dependency?
check.a: Extract the shared logic into a third bean or use events; avoid @Lazy hacks.

takeaways: Singleton by default; prototype, request and session scopes exist.
Lifecycle: instantiate, inject, Aware callbacks, post-processors, init, use, destroy; AOP proxies appear after init.
Singletons are shared across threads, so keep them stateless.

check.q: Prototype injected into a singleton: what happens?
check.a: It is created once, so you need ObjectProvider, @Lookup or a scoped proxy for a new one each time.

check.q: BeanPostProcessor vs BeanFactoryPostProcessor?
check.a: The first changes bean instances; the second changes bean definitions before instances exist.

check.q: Is a singleton bean thread-safe?
check.a: Only if it holds no mutable shared state.

takeaways: @SpringBootApplication = configuration + auto-configuration + component scan from the main package.
Auto-configuration classes apply only when their conditions match; your own beans win.
Debug what applied with the conditions evaluation report (`--debug` or Actuator).

check.q: How does Boot decide to configure a DataSource?
check.a: Conditions: the driver class is on the classpath and you have not defined a DataSource bean.

check.q: How do you see why an auto-configuration did not apply?
check.a: The conditions evaluation report.

check.q: What is a starter?
check.a: A dependency bundle that brings the libraries plus their auto-configuration.

takeaways: Request flow: filters, DispatcherServlet, handler mapping, interceptors, controller, message converters.
One @RestControllerAdvice maps exceptions to status codes and a consistent body (ProblemDetail).
Validate DTOs with @Valid; filters are servlet-level, interceptors are Spring MVC-level.

check.q: Filter vs interceptor?
check.a: A filter wraps every servlet request; an interceptor wraps handler execution and knows the controller method.

check.q: Which status for a validation failure?
check.a: 400 Bad Request.

check.q: Why not return JPA entities from controllers?
check.a: They leak internal fields, risk lazy-loading errors and couple the API to the schema.

takeaways: Entities move between transient, managed, detached and removed; managed changes flush automatically.
Make associations LAZY and fetch what each use case needs.
getReferenceById returns a proxy without a query; findById loads the row.

check.q: What is dirty checking?
check.a: At flush, Hibernate compares managed entities to their snapshots and writes the changes.

check.q: Default fetch type of @ManyToOne?
check.a: EAGER; set it to LAZY.

check.q: Why does ddl-auto=update not belong in production?
check.a: It changes schemas unpredictably; use Flyway or Liquibase migrations.

takeaways: N+1: one query for parents plus one per parent for a lazy association.
Fix with JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, batch fetching or DTO projections.
Turn off Open Session in View so lazy loading cannot hide in the view layer.

check.q: How do you detect N+1?
check.a: SQL logging or Hibernate statistics, and assert the query count in tests.

check.q: Why not JOIN FETCH two collections at once?
check.a: It creates a Cartesian product (and Hibernate rejects multiple bags).

check.q: What is OSIV and why disable it?
check.a: Open Session in View keeps the session open for the whole request, hiding lazy loads and holding connections.

takeaways: @Transactional works through a proxy: self-invocation, private and final methods bypass it.
Rollback is on RuntimeException and Error by default; checked exceptions commit unless configured.
REQUIRED joins, REQUIRES_NEW suspends and starts another; keep transactions short and without remote calls.

check.q: Why does calling a @Transactional method from the same class not start a transaction?
check.a: The call does not go through the proxy.

check.q: When use REQUIRES_NEW?
check.a: For work that must commit independently, such as an audit record.

check.q: What is UnexpectedRollbackException?
check.a: An inner REQUIRED method marked the shared transaction rollback-only, but the outer one tried to commit.

takeaways: Security is a filter chain: authenticate the request, store it in the SecurityContext, then authorise.
Configure with a SecurityFilterChain bean; for JWTs prefer the OAuth2 resource server support.
CSRF matters for cookie sessions; CORS is browser policy; store passwords with BCrypt or Argon2.

check.q: Where does Spring Security keep the current user?
check.a: In the SecurityContext, held by the SecurityContextHolder for the request.

check.q: Do you need CSRF protection for a stateless JWT API?
check.a: Not if tokens are sent in a header rather than cookies.

check.q: How do you secure a single method?
check.a: @PreAuthorize with @EnableMethodSecurity.

takeaways: AOP adds cross-cutting behaviour (transactions, caching, security) through proxies.
JDK proxies need an interface; CGLIB subclasses the class (Boot's default).
Self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so advice does not run.

check.q: Why do @Transactional and @Cacheable fail on self-calls?
check.a: The call stays inside the object and never reaches the proxy.

check.q: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB?
check.a: JDK proxies implement interfaces; CGLIB creates a subclass, so final methods cannot be advised.

check.q: Name three Spring features built on AOP.
check.a: Transactions, caching and method security.

takeaways: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups.
Conditional aggregation (`SUM(CASE WHEN ...)`) pivots rows into columns.
Prefer EXISTS over IN for correlated checks, and NOT EXISTS over NOT IN when NULLs are possible.

check.q: Why can NOT IN return no rows?
check.a: If the subquery contains a NULL, every comparison is unknown.

check.q: When use a CTE?
check.a: For readability, reuse within one query, or recursion such as hierarchies.

check.q: Where does a condition on COUNT(*) go?
check.a: In HAVING.

takeaways: Window functions compute over related rows without collapsing them.
ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK differ only on ties.
LAG and LEAD compare with neighbours; gaps and islands uses value minus ROW_NUMBER.

check.q: Top 3 salaries per department?
check.a: DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) ≤ 3.

check.q: Running total?
check.a: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY date ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING).

check.q: Window function vs GROUP BY?
check.a: GROUP BY returns one row per group; a window keeps every row and adds the computed value.

takeaways: InnoDB stores rows in the primary-key B+tree; secondary indexes hold the key plus the primary key.
Composite indexes follow the leftmost-prefix rule: equality columns first, then range or sort.
A covering index answers the query from the index alone.

check.q: Why keep primary keys short?
check.a: Every secondary index stores the primary key, so a wide key bloats all of them.

check.q: Does an index on (a, b) help `WHERE b = ?`?
check.a: Not normally; b is not a leftmost prefix.

check.q: Name two things that stop an index being used.
check.a: A function on the column, and an implicit type conversion; also a leading wildcard.

takeaways: Find slow queries first (slow log, performance_schema), then EXPLAIN them.
Watch for full scans, filesort, temporary tables, and rows examined far above rows returned.
Fix with the right index, sargable predicates, fewer columns and keyset pagination.

check.q: What does 'sargable' mean?
check.a: A predicate the engine can answer with an index seek, e.g. a range on the bare column.

check.q: EXPLAIN type ALL means?
check.a: A full table scan.

check.q: Why can SELECT * be slower?
check.a: It reads more data and prevents covering indexes.

takeaways: ACID: undo log gives atomicity, redo log gives durability, locks and MVCC give isolation.
InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ with snapshot reads; locking reads see the latest data.
Prevent lost updates with a conditional update, optimistic version, or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

check.q: Which anomaly does READ COMMITTED still allow?
check.a: Non-repeatable reads (and phantoms).

check.q: Why are long transactions harmful?
check.a: They hold locks and keep old row versions alive, slowing everyone.

check.q: What is a lost update?
check.a: Two transactions read, modify and write the same value; one write overwrites the other.

takeaways: MVCC: readers see a snapshot built from undo logs, so plain reads take no locks.
Locking reads take record, gap and next-key locks on index records.
InnoDB detects deadlocks and rolls one back; lock in a consistent order and retry.

check.q: What does a next-key lock prevent?
check.a: Inserts into the gap, which would otherwise create phantoms.

check.q: What does SKIP LOCKED give you?
check.a: Workers grab unlocked rows only, so queues scale without blocking.

check.q: A query without an index uses FOR UPDATE. Risk?
check.a: It locks many rows (index records scanned), blocking others.

takeaways: Scale in order: indexes and queries, caching, vertical scaling, read replicas, partitioning, then sharding.
Replication is usually asynchronous, so replicas lag; route read-your-writes to the primary.
Sharding splits data across servers by a key; choose a key that spreads load and keeps queries local.

check.q: Partitioning vs sharding?
check.a: Partitioning splits a table inside one server; sharding spreads data across servers.

check.q: Why does a user not see their own update?
check.a: The read went to a lagging replica.

check.q: What makes a good shard key?
check.a: High cardinality, even load, and present in most queries.

takeaways: Microservices trade simpler, independent deploys for distributed-system complexity.
Split by business capability with a database per service; avoid a distributed monolith.
A well-modularised monolith is often the right start; extract with the strangler fig pattern.

check.q: What is a distributed monolith?
check.a: Services that must deploy together or share a database, so you get the costs without the benefits.

check.q: When stay with a monolith?
check.a: Small team, unclear domain boundaries, or no need for independent scaling.

check.q: What is the strangler fig pattern?
check.a: Route traffic gradually from the old system to new services until the old part can be removed.

takeaways: Service discovery maps service names to changing addresses (Eureka, or Kubernetes Services).
An API gateway centralises routing, auth, rate limiting and TLS for clients.
Config lives outside the artifact: config server, ConfigMaps and Secrets.

check.q: Client-side vs server-side discovery?
check.a: The caller picks an instance itself, or a load balancer picks for it.

check.q: Gateway vs load balancer?
check.a: A gateway handles API concerns and routing across services; a load balancer spreads traffic across instances.

check.q: What does a service mesh add?
check.a: mTLS, retries, timeouts and telemetry in sidecars or the platform, not in code.

takeaways: Synchronous calls (REST, gRPC) when you need the answer now; messaging when the work can happen later.
Every remote call needs connect and read timeouts.
Version APIs, keep changes backward compatible, and propagate trace context.

check.q: Feign vs WebClient vs RestClient?
check.a: Feign: declarative interface; WebClient: non-blocking; RestClient: modern synchronous fluent client.

check.q: Why are timeouts mandatory?
check.a: Without them a slow dependency ties up all your threads.

check.q: When choose gRPC?
check.a: Internal, high-throughput service-to-service calls with a strict contract.

takeaways: Topics are split into partitions; the key picks the partition, and order holds only within one.
Within a consumer group each partition goes to one consumer; offsets track progress.
Delivery is at-least-once in practice, so consumers must be idempotent.

check.q: How do you keep an order's events in sequence?
check.a: Use the order id as the key so they land in one partition.

check.q: What happens with more consumers than partitions?
check.a: The extra consumers sit idle.

check.q: Why is Kafka fast?
check.a: Sequential disk writes, page cache, batching, compression and zero-copy transfer.

takeaways: Start with timeouts; retry only idempotent calls with exponential backoff and jitter.
A circuit breaker fails fast when a dependency is down; a bulkhead limits concurrent calls to it.
Always define the fallback: cached data, a default, or a clear error.

check.q: Circuit breaker states?
check.a: Closed, open, half-open.

check.q: Why add jitter to retries?
check.a: So clients do not retry in lockstep and hammer the recovering service together.

check.q: What does a bulkhead protect?
check.a: Your threads, so one slow dependency cannot consume them all.

takeaways: Avoid 2PC; use a saga of local transactions with compensations.
Choreography reacts to events; orchestration has one coordinator; pick orchestration for long flows.
The outbox pattern publishes events reliably; idempotent consumers handle redelivery.

check.q: Why avoid 2PC?
check.a: It blocks on a coordinator, is slow, and most brokers and NoSQL stores do not support it.

check.q: What is a compensating transaction?
check.a: A step that semantically undoes an earlier one, such as refunding a charge.

check.q: Outbox vs CDC?
check.a: Outbox writes events to a table in the same transaction; CDC (e.g. Debezium) streams them from the database log.

takeaways: Default change detection checks the whole tree after every async event (via Zone.js).
OnPush checks a component only on new input references, its own events, signals it reads, or when marked.
Zoneless (default for new apps in v21) relies on signals and explicit notifications.

check.q: Why does mutating an array input not update an OnPush child?
check.a: The reference did not change; pass a new array.

check.q: What triggers change detection with Zone.js?
check.a: Any patched async task completing: events, timers, promises, XHR.

check.q: How would you optimise change detection?
check.a: OnPush, signals, `track` in @for, pure pipes, and moving work out of templates.

takeaways: signal holds state, computed derives cached values, effect runs side effects.
linkedSignal is writable state that resets when its source changes; resource loads async data into signals.
Use signals for state and RxJS for event streams; bridge with toSignal and toObservable.

check.q: computed vs effect?
check.a: computed returns a derived value; effect performs side effects and returns nothing.

check.q: When linkedSignal?
check.a: A selection that should reset when the list it depends on changes.

check.q: Do signals need unsubscribing?
check.a: No; there is no subscription to clean up.

takeaways: Injectors form a hierarchy: element injectors up the component tree, then environment injectors.
providedIn: 'root' gives a tree-shakable singleton; component providers give one instance per component.
inject() works only in an injection context (constructor, field initialiser, factory).

check.q: How do you get a separate service instance per component?
check.a: List it in the component's providers.

check.q: What is an InjectionToken for?
check.a: Injecting non-class values such as configuration.

check.q: Where can you call inject()?
check.a: In an injection context: constructors, field initialisers, provider factories.

takeaways: Observables are lazy streams; cold ones start per subscriber, hot ones share.
switchMap cancels, mergeMap runs in parallel, concatMap queues, exhaustMap ignores while busy.
Avoid leaks with the async pipe, toSignal or takeUntilDestroyed.

check.q: Which operator for a search-as-you-type box?
check.a: debounceTime then switchMap, so older requests are cancelled.

check.q: BehaviorSubject vs Subject?
check.a: BehaviorSubject holds a current value and replays it to new subscribers.

check.q: Which operator prevents double form submission?
check.a: exhaustMap.

takeaways: Measure first, then separate load-time from runtime problems.
Load time: lazy routes, @defer, smaller bundles. Runtime: OnPush, signals, track in @for, virtual scrolling.
Network: cache, paginate and avoid duplicate requests.

check.q: What does @defer do?
check.a: Loads a template block and its dependencies lazily, on a trigger such as viewport.

check.q: Why use track in @for?
check.a: So Angular reuses DOM nodes instead of recreating them when the list changes.

check.q: A 10,000-row list is slow. Fix?
check.a: Virtual scrolling (CDK) plus OnPush.

takeaways: A closure keeps access to its outer scope after that scope returns.
Used for private state, factories, memoisation, debounce and throttle.
Watch for stale closures and retained memory.

check.q: Write debounce in words.
check.a: Keep a timer in a closure; each call clears it and sets a new one; run the function when it fires.

check.q: Why does a closure cause a leak?
check.a: It keeps referenced variables, and anything they reference, alive.

check.q: Debounce vs throttle?
check.a: Debounce waits for a pause; throttle runs at most once per interval.

takeaways: One call stack; async callbacks wait in queues.
After each macrotask, all microtasks (promises) run before the next macrotask (timers, events).
Long synchronous work blocks rendering and input.

check.q: Order: setTimeout 0 vs Promise.then?
check.a: The promise callback runs first; it is a microtask.

check.q: Why can a page freeze?
check.a: A long synchronous task blocks the single thread.

check.q: Is setTimeout(fn, 0) immediate?
check.a: No; it queues a macrotask after the current task and all microtasks.

takeaways: A promise is pending, then fulfilled or rejected, once.
Promise.all fails fast; allSettled waits for all; race and any take the first.
await in a loop runs sequentially; use Promise.all for independent work.

check.q: all vs allSettled?
check.a: all rejects on the first failure; allSettled reports every outcome.

check.q: What does an async function return?
check.a: Always a promise.

check.q: Why can awaiting in a loop be slow?
check.a: Each await waits for the previous call; independent calls should run in parallel.

takeaways: Know methods, idempotency, and status classes; 401 is unauthenticated, 403 is forbidden.
HTTP/1.1 reuses connections, HTTP/2 multiplexes streams on one TCP connection, HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
Caching headers (Cache-Control, ETag) avoid repeat transfers.

check.q: Which methods are idempotent?
check.a: GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS; POST is not.

check.q: What problem does HTTP/3 solve over HTTP/2?
check.a: TCP head-of-line blocking: a lost packet stalls only its own stream.

check.q: What is an ETag for?
check.a: Conditional requests: the server returns 304 Not Modified if the content is unchanged.

takeaways: DNS resolves through resolver, root, TLD and authoritative servers, with caching by TTL.
Typing a URL: DNS, TCP and TLS handshakes, HTTP request, response, parse, fetch assets, render.
Answer at the depth the interviewer wants and offer to go deeper on any step.

check.q: Recursive vs iterative DNS query?
check.a: The resolver does the whole lookup for you (recursive) by asking each server in turn (iterative).

check.q: What does HSTS do?
check.a: Tells the browser to use HTTPS only for the site.

check.q: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv4 address?
check.a: An A record (AAAA for IPv6).

takeaways: A process has its own address space; threads share their process's memory.
A context switch saves and restores CPU state; it costs time and cache warmth.
Concurrency is dealing with many things at once; parallelism is doing them at the same time.

check.q: Why are threads cheaper than processes?
check.a: They share memory, so creating and switching them needs less setup.

check.q: What is a zombie process?
check.a: A finished child whose exit status its parent has not collected.

check.q: Concurrency vs parallelism?
check.a: Interleaving tasks vs running them simultaneously on multiple cores.

takeaways: STAR: situation and task briefly, actions in detail (about 60%), result with numbers.
Say 'I', be specific, explain your reasoning, and end with what you learned.
Build a story bank of 6-8 real stories in week 1 and practise them out loud.

check.q: How much of a STAR answer should be actions?
check.a: About 60%.

check.q: Why say 'I' not 'we'?
check.a: Interviewers grade your contribution, not the team's.

check.q: Which stories belong in the bank?
check.a: Incident, conflict, ownership, ambiguity, mentoring, failure, and a hard technical problem.

takeaways: Describe projects by the client's business and scale, the architecture, your ownership, and measured impact.
Turn tasks into outcomes: what changed for users or the business, with numbers.
Prepare a 60-second pitch and deep-dive answers for your main project.

check.q: What are the four layers of a project description?
check.a: Business context and scale, architecture, your ownership, highlights with impact.

check.q: No dashboards: how do you find numbers?
check.a: Estimate from logs, tickets, release notes or before-and-after timings, and say they are estimates.

check.q: What should you avoid saying?
check.a: 'I just did what the client asked' or vague 'we worked on' answers.

takeaways: Tell me about yourself: present, past, future in 60-90 seconds.
Why switch: move towards ownership, scale and product impact; never criticise your employer.
Why us: product, engineering challenge, your fit, and growth.

check.q: How long should 'tell me about yourself' be?
check.a: 60-90 seconds.

check.q: 'Is it about money?' How do you answer?
check.a: Acknowledge pay matters, then focus on the role, ownership and growth.

check.q: Why leave after only 2 years?
check.a: You have learned what the role offers and want more scale, ownership and product depth.

takeaways: Amazon grades stories against its Leadership Principles, with a Bar Raiser in the loop.
Map each story to 2-3 principles (Ownership, Dive Deep, Customer Obsession, Deliver Results, Disagree and Commit).
Expect follow-up probes for detail, data and what you would do differently.

check.q: What is a Bar Raiser?
check.a: An interviewer from outside the team who checks the hire raises the bar and can veto.

check.q: Which principle fits a disagreement story?
check.a: Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit.

check.q: What do LP follow-ups look for?
check.a: Specific actions, data, and your own judgement.
